title: Ezra 9:1–4
context: Some time after Ezra’s arrival in Jerusalem, leaders report to him that many among the returned exiles, including priests, Levites, and leading officials, have married women from the surrounding peoples, whose practices the text calls abominations. The list of peoples recalls older lists in the law (compare Deuteronomy 7:1–4 and 23:3–8). The stated concern is covenant faithfulness and the danger of idolatry, as the following prayer makes explicit (9:11–12). Ezra tears his garments, pulls out hair from his head and beard, and sits appalled until the evening offering, joined by those who tremble at God’s words.

verses.text: Now when these things were done, the princes came near to me, saying, “The people of Israel, the priests, and the Levites have not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands, following their abominations, even those of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, the Ammonites, the Moabites, the Egyptians, and the Amorites.
verses.arminianNotes: Leaders report that the people, priests, and Levites have not separated from the peoples of the lands and their abominations. Arminian readers note that the concern is presented as faithfulness to the covenant amid surrounding practices of false worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the list of peoples as recalling Deuteronomy 7:1–4, where intermarriage is forbidden because it would turn Israel to other gods. Shared ground: both traditions read the stated issue as covenant fidelity and idolatry, not ethnicity as such.

verses.text: For they have taken of their daughters for themselves and for their sons, so that the holy offspring have mixed themselves with the peoples of the lands. Yes, the hand of the princes and rulers has been chief in this trespass.”
verses.arminianNotes: The report says the holy offspring have mixed with the peoples, and that leaders were foremost in this trespass. Arminian readers note that responsibility is placed especially on those who should have guided the community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the phrase “holy offspring” as recalling Israel’s calling to be set apart for God. Both traditions read the verse as the leaders’ charge, and they avoid blaming the women as a class; the narrator frames it as Israel’s trespass.

verses.text: When I heard this thing, I tore my garment and my robe, and pulled the hair out of my head and of my beard, and sat down confounded.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezra tears his garment and robe, pulls hair from his head and beard, and sits appalled. Arminian readers see deep personal grief over the community’s sin, expressed in traditional signs of mourning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Ezra identifying with the people’s guilt rather than standing apart from it. Shared ground: both traditions read Ezra’s response as heartfelt sorrow, and note that the narrative here shifts to his own first-person account.

verses.text: Then everyone who trembled at the words of the God of Israel were assembled to me because of the trespass of the exiles; and I sat confounded until the evening offering.
verses.arminianNotes: Those who tremble at God’s words gather to Ezra as he sits appalled until the evening offering. Arminian readers note that a group within the community shares his concern and responds to God’s word with reverence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see trembling at God’s word as a mark of true piety, compare Isaiah 66:2 by reference. Both traditions read the verse as describing a faithful core who support Ezra’s grief and await what he will do.
